title: Existentialism’s 21st‑Century Continuations - Technology & AI Ethics
content_html:
Existentialism’s 21st‑Century Continuations - Technology & AI Ethics

  • Substrate: Technical infrastructures (databases, platforms) operate as external memory substrates for persons and societies (extended mind, tertiary retention).
  • Mind / Process: Algorithmic curation and tools co‑shape Select–Change–Reconstruct in personal memory (attention capture, reminders, search, photos); machine unlearning as engineered forgetting.
  • Language / Expression: Platformised collective memory (feeds, trends) conditions narrative identity and public remembrance.
  • Meaning / Void / Infinite: Existential responsibility and authenticity under datafication; alignment as interpretive (phenomenological) rather than purely optimization.

Externalised memory

extended mind & tertiary retention

Contemporary philosophy of mind frames digital storage and tools as constitutive parts of cognition rather than mere aids, via the extended/embodied mind debates. The Stanford Encyclopedia surveys how cognition and even acts like remembering can be partly realized in external structures.

Media philosophy deepens this: tertiary retention (Stiegler) names technical supports of memory that reshape primary (perceptual) and secondary (recollective) retention; digital platforms thereby pre‑format what is recallable.

Algorithmic memory

platforms as co‑authors of collective remembering

Digital memory studies show a shift from “collective memory” to “memory of the multitude” and “connective memory,” where platform logics (ranking, recommendation, moderation) decide what persists, resurfaces, or vanishes. Recent reviews track how social media transforms public remembrance and forgetting.

Existential stakes: algorithmic mediation affects authenticity and responsibility: what one can own and answer for depends on discoverability and framing of past acts—altering the horizon of being‑with‑others.

Governance of forgetting

legal erasure and machine unlearning

The EU’s Right to Erasure (GDPR Art. 17) recognises the ethical need to forget under certain conditions (e.g., consent withdrawal, purpose exhausted). But legal erasure requires technical procedures: hence machine unlearning, the science of removing data influence from trained models. Surveys (2023–2025) catalogue centralized, federated, and verification methods and open problems.

Existential stakes: the possibility (or impossibility) of engineered forgetting recalibrates personal and social responsibility, forgiveness, and identity continuity within digital lifeworlds.

Alignment through phenomenology

respecting lived memory

Beyond statistical alignment, phenomenological approaches argue AI should be designed around lived experience (values, technological mediation, materiality). Han (2021/2022) proposes alignment principles grounded in phenomenology—reframing data traces as sedimented memories that require interpretive, dialogical design.

Existential stakes: alignment is not merely goal matching but a practice of attunement to human meaning, responsibility, and ambiguity.

Practical patterns

  • Treat platform infrastructures as memory substrates; discuss tertiary retention and externalism.
  • machine unlearning as engineered forgetting.
  • algorithmic memory audits (e.g., search/feed replication studies) to surface platform effects on public remembrance.
  • Fold phenomenological alignment into the existential responsibility: authenticity under datafication; legal vs. technical forgetting.
